extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, scientists, and philosophers of science interested in principles for constructing scientific classifications
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for forming scientific (natural) classifications and nomenclatures, and for arranging natural groups into series to facilitate inductive inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all affinities before placing an object
rubrics_metrics.description: “can not determine the group in which any one object can most conveniently be placed, without taking into consideration all the varieties of existing objects, all at least which have any degree of affinity with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assign an object to a class in isolation; classification decisions require surveying all objects that show any affinity, since relative position depends on the whole aggregate of related objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using only simple, immediately perceptible properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial attempts are likely to select properties which are simple, easily conceived, and perceptible on a first view (e.g. Tournefort’s corolla-shape; Linnæus’s stamens/pistils), but such selections are seldom adapted to scientific ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple convenience-based characters may help immediate identification but often fail to group objects that share many important properties; avoid letting ease of perception determine scientific classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select properties that allow many and important general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ends of scientific classification are best answered, when the objects are formed into groups respecting which a greater number of general propositions can be made, and those propositions more important...than could be made respecting any other groups.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classificatory bases that maximize both the number and the importance of common, generalizable assertions about members of the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal properties or sure marks of other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: “The properties, therefore, according to which objects are classified, should, if possible, be those which are causes of many other properties; or, at any rate, which are sure marks of them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible choose traits that are causes (or reliable indicators) of many other traits, since these both ground explanation and point to further, discoverable properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify by natural (not merely technical/artificial) affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: A Natural classification corresponds to the spontaneous tendencies of the mind by placing together objects most similar in their general aspect, as opposed to technical systems that group by an arbitrarily selected circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a system’s scientific character by the number and importance of properties that can be asserted in common of group members; avoid artificial groupings that mix dissimilar things or separate close affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid classifications that distort habits of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitually thinking of plants by trivial or irrelevant characters (e.g. number of stamens) prevents thinking of groups with more numerous or important shared properties and is ‘mischievous.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that persistent use of an artificial scheme can bias research and observation; choose classifications that steer habitual attention toward genuinely important shared properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unobvious but important properties when necessary, with accessible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups must often be founded on unobvious properties of greater importance, but there should be some other property or set of properties, more readily recognizable by the observer, which co-exist with and may be received as marks of the underlying properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the true basis of grouping is internal/unobvious, ensure there are external, recognizable correlates (diagnostics) so practitioners can identify group membership without destructive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require extensive empirical knowledge for good classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive knowledge of the properties of objects is necessary for making a good classification; classification and knowledge tend mutually and indefinitely to the improvement of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat classification as an iterative, knowledge-building process: better classifications arise from broader knowledge, and good classifications focus attention to discover new properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor classification to the purpose or practical end
rubrics_metrics.description: Each science or art forms its classification of things according to the properties which fall within its special cognizance or which it must take account of to accomplish its peculiar practical end (e.g., farmer: useful plants vs weeds; geologist: fossil stratigraphy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that multiple valid classifications may exist; choose the classificatory basis appropriate to your explanatory or practical goal, and be explicit about that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define classes by characters, not merely by type resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Though groups are suggested by types, they are determined by characters; the problem is to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer enumerated diagnostic characters that indicate membership and predict other properties, rather than relying solely on resemblance to a mental exemplar or 'type'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for exceptions and near-members in natural groups
rubrics_metrics.description: A class may include species that lack one or more universal characters (exceptions) but resemble the class more than any other; classes are constituted by universal characters and most of those which admit of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design definitions to capture all universally present characters and the majority of common ones, accepting a limited number of exceptions when overall affinity is stronger with the group than with alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute classes so they point to distinctions of Kind where present
rubrics_metrics.description: Every natural classification shall recognize and adopt into itself all distinctions of Kind which exist among the objects it professes to classify; to pass over distinctions of Kind is subversive of the Natural Method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'Kinds' (differences running through whole nature) exist, ensure classifications respect those boundaries; avoid substituting merely definite differences that do not imply further, unknown differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that many higher taxa are defined by limited but important characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few genera or families can be pronounced with certainty to be Kinds; genera and families may be eminently natural though marked out from one another by properties limited in number if those properties are important and give more internal than external resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand that every taxonomic level be a metaphysical 'Kind'; practical naturalness can arise from a small set of important characters that produce cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nomenclature to convey as much information as practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nomenclature is a system of the names of Kinds; the only merit beyond definition is to convey, by construction, as much information as possible about the proximate natural affinities or distinctive characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer names whose formation suggests the proximate group (e.g., binary genus+species), and where possible encode diagnostic information (as in chemical formulae for compounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ binary (or appropriate hierarchical) nomenclature to economize memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary nomenclature (genus + specific epithet) makes names convey proximate affinities and economizes on the number of distinct names required as species numbers grow; ternary systems are possible but binary is usually sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a hierarchical name construction (at least genus+species) to reduce naming burden and to reflect natural groupings; increase depth only if necessary for clarity (as in some mineralogical schemes).

rubrics_metrics.name: When studying a specific phenomenon, group all kinds exhibiting it
rubrics_metrics.description: For a classification intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon, first bring into one class all Kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon, in whatever variety of forms or degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble all instances where the phenomenon occurs, regardless of other differing properties, to provide the proper dataset for inductive inference about the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange those kinds in a series by degree of the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, arrange those Kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most of it, and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering instances by degree of manifestation prepares the data for methods of concomitant variations and helps reveal causal or correlational relations across degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a type (exemplar) for special inductive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: When the classification is made for the express purpose of a special inductive inquiry, it is not optional but necessary that we should establish a type-species or genus, namely, the one which exhibits in the most eminent degree the particular phenomenon under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an exemplar that most clearly exhibits the phenomenon to orient the series and highlight concomitant variations across other instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the series to apply the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of a set of objects in a series according to degrees in which they exhibit a fact is the ordering implied in the Method of Concomitant Variations (facts that increase or diminish together are cause/effect or effects of a common cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct series deliberately to enable identification of concomitant increases/decreases; this ordering is often essential when experimental separation of co-occurring circumstances is limited.
